# Dossier: LTL freight-invoice audit for small and mid-size shippers

Research date 2026-10-25. About 40 searches and fetches. Evidence tags: **[P]** primary (statute, regulation, carrier or company's own page), **[S]** secondary or dataset with a stated method, **[V]** vendor claim, **[est]** my calculation or inference. Where a site blocked my fetcher I say the figure comes from a search summary. The project's own FACT-CHECK found search summaries inventing quotes, so those items are weak.

## 1. Verdict

The problem is real and the law is on the shipper's side, but three things limit this as a business.

1. **The front door is crowded and free.** Every LTL-capable firm I could read that states its model offers a path with no fee before recovery. A free tool from Warp, a free tier from LanePilot and a "first audit free, 15%" shop (Eller) all sit in the exact niche. The $500 diagnostic is an outlier. The project's own offer-v2 research (2026-10-25) reached the same conclusion, and my check agrees.
2. **Unit economics are thin at the small end.** My model (section 3): a shipper with $100k of LTL spend yields about $300 a year in fees at a central case. A $1M shipper yields about $3,000. About 20 such clients make roughly $60k a year before carrier denials.
3. **Nothing is validated.** Revenue is $0 and the project's own playbook says no cold calls happened in 2.5 months. Recovered dollars per client-month and whether strangers send invoices are both unknown.

My call: **viable side income, unproven as a scalable company.** It is worth a six-week test only if the front door becomes free-first or contingency-only, the target moves to $500k–$5M LTL spend, and a data-asset path (section 9) is designed in from the start.

## 2. Competitors serving small and mid shippers

| Firm | Serves | Price | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Eller Audit | Two-founder AI plus contract specialist; all modes | First audit free; **15% fixed**; claims rivals charge 30–50% (unsupported) | [P](https://www.elleraudit.com/savings-calculator), [LTL page](https://www.elleraudit.com/ltl-freight-audit) |
| Lojistic | Self-serve; audit covers LTL | **Free forever** audit with 100-day history; contingency 29%, or $99/mo + 19%, $389/mo + 9%, $5,959/mo + 0% | [P](https://lojistic.com/pricing) |
| LanePilot | Small/mid manufacturers and distributors; one named founder, Erie PA | Free: 5 quotes, 7 audits/month; dispute letters included; "does not file on your behalf"; paid prices unlisted | [P](https://lanepilottech.com/) |
| Warp | Free reweigh/reclass checker against your BOL | Free | [P](https://www.wearewarp.com/tools/reweigh-reclass-audit) |
| AFS Logistics | "Big and small" | Post-audit, no price; claims up to 8% of spend; 1,800 clients, 380 staff | [P](https://afs.net/service/post-audit/) |
| WAI, Goodman-Reichwald-Dodge | Small contingency post-audit shops | "Percentage of amount recovered," unstated | [P](https://waionline.com/freight-post-audit); [GRD](https://www.freightbillauditor.com/PostAuditServices) (read by offer-v2, not re-fetched) |
| TLI, GLT, Auditec | Mid shippers, forwarders | Quote or free look; TLI wants an NDA plus 3 months of invoices | read in project's [offer-v2](/Users/asherperemel/projects/freight-audit/research/gtm-oct/offer-v2.md) |
| Loop | Enterprise; $95M Series C Apr 2026; about $44M ARR (Sacra estimate) | Undisclosed | [S](https://sacra.com/c/loop) |
| Cass, Intelligent Audit, CT Logistics | Enterprise | Undisclosed | project research |
| Lighthouz AI (YC S24) | Brokers, LTL and FTL bill audit | Seed stage | [V](https://ycombinator.com/companies/lighthouz-ai) (search summary) |

- **Not LTL competitors:** Refund Retriever (UPS/FedEx, 40–50% ladder) and ShipScience (parcel, 35%), per pages read by the project's offer-v2 and not re-fetched by me: [Refund Retriever](https://www.refundretriever.com/pricing/), [ShipScience](https://www.shipscience.com/pricing/).
- **Built-in audit:** FreightPOP has an audit module aimed at larger buyers. I could not confirm audit in Freightview, Shipwell or Freightquote. 3PLs such as TI and CT bundle audit into managed transportation.
- **Carrier-side location data:** Shiplify says 21 of the top 25 LTL carriers use its accessorial and location database ([V](https://blog.shiplify.com/shiplify-help/location-lookup-tool-empower-shippers)). It partnered with FreightSnap on 2026-07-01 ([V](https://freightsnap.com/freightsnap-and-shiplify-partner-to-build-greater-trust-in-ltl-freight/)). This is a risk to the "accessorial never rendered" thesis, because carriers may increasingly pre-validate location-type fees. Its claim is unverified.
- **Free-tier history gap:** Lojistic's free plan keeps 100 days of data, shorter than the 180-day claim window. Paid tiers keep 5 years.
- **Minimums:** none published for small shippers. A search summary of Inbound Logistics (page blocked) puts outsourcing thresholds between $500k and $10M, so treat as noise.
- **Fee norm in the wider category:** AP recovery audits charge [20–30%](https://www.apexanalytix.com/resources/blog/recovery-audit-cost/) [V]. A Texas Comptroller report cites an [industry average of 20–40%](https://fmx.cpa.texas.gov/fm/audit/recovery/rpt2014/Recovery_Audit_2014.pdf) [S, 2014]. So 20% is in range, and 15% (Eller) undercuts it.

## 3. How many shippers, and what a client is worth

**No source publishes a count.** What exists:

- US LTL revenue was **$51.8B in 2025**, down from a $58.7B peak in 2022, with 649,796 average daily shipments (SJ Consulting via [JOC](https://magazine.joc.com/july-6-2026/0109987001782412674/p34) and Supply Chain 247; fetch blocked, from search summaries).
- XPO reported **38,000 LTL customers and $4.8B revenue** in 2025 ([XPO deck](https://investors.xpo.com/static-files/534c0d3b-fb12-480a-b1cc-4242f31a917b); blocked, search summary). That is about $126k per customer [est].
- NAM says [74% of US manufacturers have under 20 employees](https://nam.org/member-services/smm-membership/) [P]. A NAM sheet citing Census puts firms at about 239,000 (search summary), so roughly 62,000 manufacturers have 20 or more employees [est].
- Revenue per shipment is about $320 ($51.8B ÷ 649,796 × 250 days) [est]. So $100k is about 6 shipments a week and $5M is about 63 a day.

**My triangulation [est]:** XPO holds about 9% of US LTL revenue. Scaling its customer count implies roughly 410,000 carrier-customer relationships, or 80,000–140,000 distinct LTL shippers at 3–5 carriers each. The mean is then $370k–$630k, and the median is far lower. I put the $100k–$5M band at **roughly 25,000–70,000 shippers**, of which perhaps 10,000–30,000 spend over $500k. Treat this as order of magnitude. Market size is not the constraint, since the business needs 20–100 clients. Reach and trust are.

**Per-client fees [est, before carrier denials, 20% fee]:**

| LTL spend | Recoverable 0.5% / 1.5% / 3% | Annual fee | One-time backlog fee (180 days) |
|---|---|---|---|
| $100k | $500 / $1.5k / $3k | $100 / $300 / $600 | $50 / $150 / $300 |
| $500k | $2.5k / $7.5k / $15k | $500 / $1.5k / $3k | $250 / $750 / $1.5k |
| $2M | $10k / $30k / $60k | $2k / $6k / $12k | $1k / $3k / $6k |

Two corollaries. The window is rolling, so the "backlog" is only six months and the rest is ongoing monthly work. And the $500 diagnostic rarely clears $500 of findings below about $400k of spend: one month at $100k spend is about $8k, so 1.5% is $125. The contract already makes the $500 owed only if findings reach $500 ([contract](/Users/asherperemel/projects/freight-audit/contracts/engagement-terms.md)), so in practice it is a contingent fee with a floor.

## 4. Error and recovery rates

| Figure | Source | Grade |
|---|---|---|
| **4.5% of about 250,000 LTL invoices had errors** (11,881). Mix: accessorials 42.8%, fuel 14.4%, class 12.3%, discount/minimum/rate 10.3%. The count implies about 264,000 invoices, so the numbers do not quite reconcile. | [AFS blog, Mar 2024](https://afs.net/blog/stats-incredible-common-ltl-invoice-errors/) | S, best available; AFS client invoices, no period |
| Median recovery **2–5% of annual LTL spend**; class-error win rate 70–82%, accessorial 60–75% | [Eller LTL page](https://www.elleraudit.com/ltl-freight-audit) | V, win rates unsupported |
| LTL recovery 3–7% of spend; spot check catches about 40% of a full audit | [Warp calculator](https://www.wearewarp.com/tools/freight-audit-savings-calculator) | V, unnamed benchmarks |
| Average invoice inaccuracy **20.8% across all modes**, self-reported, n=77, "small" means under $500M revenue | [JOC 2020](https://www.joc.com/sites/default/files/u45421/Whitepapers/Freight-Payment-report-78441.pdf) | S, weak, large shippers |
| "80% of carrier invoices contain errors," "10% of spend lost" | [Loop site](https://www.loop.com) | V, marketing |
| 25% of shipments re-rated at some shippers; one cut re-rates to 1% with a dimensioner | [ODFL](https://www.odfl.com/us/en/resources/OD-Outlook/Accurate-Freight-Data-in-LTL-Shipping.html) | P/anecdote |
| 13.2% LTL spend cut, 35% fewer reclass disputes (bundled with process changes) | [Intelligent Audit](https://www.intelligentaudit.com/case-studies/reducing-ltl-spend-through-freight-class-accuracy-and-audit-controls) | V |

**Inference [est]:** if 4.5% of invoices carry an error worth 10–25% of a roughly $320 invoice, errors equal 0.5–1.1% of spend. That sits under the vendor 3–8%. Plan on **0.5–3%**, and let the first three teardowns settle it. I found **no published carrier claim-approval rate** and no independent LTL study.

## 5. How these shippers buy, and who signs

- JOC's 2020 survey (n=77): the decision-maker on audit/payment technology was logistics and finance together (60.5%), logistics alone (27.9%) or finance alone (11.6%). Nearly two-thirds outsource audit or payment. Small and mid shippers reported **$19.49 to process an invoice versus $10.74 for large shippers**, and in-house $18.32 versus outsourced $6.26 ([JOC](https://www.joc.com/sites/default/files/u45421/Whitepapers/Freight-Payment-report-78441.pdf)). "Small" there means under $500M revenue, far larger than Asher's targets.
- No source covers owner-run $5–100M manufacturers. My inference: a traffic or shipping manager evaluates, the owner or controller approves, and at the smallest firms they are one person.
- **Data access is the barrier.** TLI wants an NDA plus three months of invoices first (per offer-v2). Eller and the project's offer lower this with a free first look.
- **Carriers force an agency structure.** TForce says [only the payer of the original charges can file](https://www.tforcefreight.com/ltl/apps/OverchargeClaimInformation). XPO needs the invoice paid, the BOL and delivery receipt, and accepts up to 100 PROs per submission ([XPO, Feb 2026](https://www.xpo.com/cdn/files/s1/Overcharge_Claim_Process_02-24-26.pdf)). So a signed authorization and filing in the client's name are required, as WAI does.
- Reach channels already researched in the project: MEP centers, trade associations, fractional CFOs. My inference: Asher's mentor (an AV-integration founder) is the strongest credibility transfer, since AV racks and displays are heavy, commercial-dock LTL freight. That fit is unverified.

## 6. Can an 18-year-old credibly sell this?

**Yes to owner-run shippers under $5M, with evidence instead of a résumé.**

- The closest analogs lean on experience Asher lacks: Eller cites 20 years of Fortune 500 contract work ([site](https://www.elleraudit.com/)), LanePilot "nearly a decade inside LTL freight." He needs substitutes: a free teardown on the prospect's own invoices, a published technical reference, and tools that run locally. The project has these. One edge is checkable: the NMFC density scale changed on 2025-07-19, and the project's FACT-CHECK found its own playbook table stale, so any tool must use the new 13-tier scale.
- **Why contingency helps:** it caps the buyer's risk at time and data, which is the only thing a skeptical owner loses. It is also the category norm (section 2). It does not remove the data-sharing worry, so the NDA and "nothing leaves your machine" point matter.
- **Licensing:** the broker definition in [49 CFR 371.2](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/49/371.2) covers arranging transportation. Pure invoice auditing does not arrange it, so I found no licence requirement, but this is my reading, not legal advice. Do not add booking or carrier selection.
- Age of majority is 18 in most states but [19 in Alabama and Nebraska and 21 in Mississippi](https://www.policygenius.com/estate-planning/age-of-majority-by-state/) (secondary source). Check Asher's state.
- Not credible: enterprise or regulated buyers, and any claim of clients or references.

## 7. The legal points

- **180 days.** [49 USC 13710(a)(3)(B)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/49/13710) [P]: "A shipper must contest the original bill or subsequent bill within 180 days of receipt of the bill in order to have the right to contest such charges." Subparagraph (A) holds carriers to the same 180 days for extra charges, and (a)(1) lets the shipper demand the rate, classification, rules and practices behind a charge.
- ***Southern Furniture Leasing v. YRC*, 989 F.3d 1141 (10th Cir. Mar. 3, 2021)** affirmed dismissal of a putative overcharge class action on the 180-day ground ([Leagle](https://www.leagle.com/decision/infco20210303045), opinion text blocked; holding from a Justia summary). The window is enforced even against class claims.
- **Part 378.** Carriers acknowledge within 30 days ([§378.7](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/49/378.7)) and "pay, decline to pay, or settle" within 60 days, with written reasons ([§378.8](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/49/378.8)). Carrier pages drift from this. XPO says 60 days. TForce says "pay, refuse or amend within 120 days," and counts receipt as 10 days after tender, which shortens the shipper's clock. XPO requires prior payment.
- **§14101(b) waivers.** Parties may ["expressly waive any or all rights and remedies under this part"](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/49/14101) in writing, except registration, insurance and safety fitness. I found **no decision** applying a waiver to the 180-day window. Eller's page says carriers cannot contract below 180 days, which I could not verify given this clause. Read every pricing agreement for waiver language before promising a deadline.
- **Suit deadline.** [§14705(b)](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/49/14705): 18 months to sue, a different clock from the 180-day contest.
- **NMFC.** Docket 2025-1 (effective 2025-07-19) introduced a 13-tier density scale. ODFL reports about 2,000 items moved to density-only and NMFTA expects 70–80% of freight to be density-classed ([ODFL](https://www.odfl.com/us/en/resources/OD-Outlook/Accurate-Freight-Data-in-LTL-Shipping.html)). More freight is now decided by measured dimensions, which raises the value of the shipper's own dimension evidence.

## 8. Can AI audit the unstructured documents?

**Yes in principle, and it is the strongest differentiator. It is not yet proven in practice.**

- **Why documents matter:** carriers require the BOL and delivery receipt to pay a claim (XPO above). A rate-file check cannot say whether a liftgate was used. Loop says it uses LLMs to ingest documents and reconcile them to contracts, but publishes no accuracy data ([Sacra](https://sacra.com/c/loop)).
- **Capability:** an AIMultiple test of 14 models on 100 cursive samples scored Gemini 3 Pro Preview at 100% semantic similarity, with GPT-5 and olmOCR-2 also in the top group ([benchmark](https://aimultiple.com/handwriting-recognition); small, similarity-based). A search summary of [arXiv 2502.20295](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.20295) puts the best model's character error at about 6–9% on historical multi-page handwriting (I could not confirm the figures from the abstract). I found **no freight-specific benchmark** for signatures, driver notes or stamps. A hand-labelled test set of 100–200 PODs would be Asher's first proof point.
- **Limits:** the shipper must obtain the PODs. The carrier's scale and dimensioner record controls reweighs, and a carrier executive told [FreightWaves](https://www.freightwaves.com/news/ltl-suit-against-yrc-spotlights-reweighing-practices) that reweighs rarely favor the customer. Shiplify sells its location data to carriers. AI should draft findings, and a human should approve each claim.
- **Whitespace, partly:** Lighthouz targets brokers, Loop targets enterprise, and LanePilot checks invoices against quotes and drafts dispute letters for small shippers. I found no one positioning document-grounded accessorial verification for direct shippers in the $500k–$5M band, but Eller's LTL page already lists "accessorial billed without BOL evidence" as a failure mode. This is a differentiator in degree, not in kind.

## 9. Service to scalable product or data asset

1. **Service (0–10 clients).** The audit engine already has about 20 checks and a large test suite.
2. **Self-serve plus paid dispute packets.** Lojistic's ladder (a monthly fee buys down the contingency rate) and LanePilot's free tier are the templates. Free audit, paid filing, contingency on large claims.
3. **Data assets.** Shiplify sells location data to 21 of 25 carriers (claim). Cass publishes a [monthly freight index](https://cassinfo.com/freight-audit-payment/cass-transportation-indexes/may-2024) built from its payment data. Loop raised $95M as a "Logistics Data Platform." Candidates for Asher [est]: (a) a **claim-outcome database** (carrier × reason × evidence × result × days to pay), (b) a quarterly **carrier accessorial-error benchmark**, usable as PR and lead generation, (c) a labelled BOL/POD corpus.
4. **Blocker:** the current contract promises not to use client data for other clients ([contract](/Users/asherperemel/projects/freight-audit/contracts/engagement-terms.md)). Add a de-identified aggregate-use clause now, before client one.
5. **Exits:** consolidators buy platforms, as in Cass/AcuAudit ([Jan 2025](https://www.freightwaves.com/news/cass-acquires-ocean-airfreight-audit-platform)), Trax/EM6 (Nov 2025, search summary) and AFS/DTA (2022). I found no multiples. A 30–50 client recovery shop is more likely to be a tuck-in or acqui-hire than a platform.

## 10. Test before committing

Six weeks inside his 10–15 weekly hours. Email 40 verified prospects, then call. Offer a free first look, with 20% on recovery and no fee before it. Get three invoice sets. Measure **collectible dollars per client-month and days to carrier decision**. Continue if at least two of three clients show 1% or more of spend collectible (about $170 a month in fees at $1M spend). Stop or reshape if the median is under 0.5%. The project's playbook expects roughly one invoice-sender per 40 prospects (range 0.4–3 per 40), so three sets needs about 120 contacts at the central rate.

## 11. Gaps

- No published count of US LTL shippers by spend band, and no claim-approval rate. Both come only from the first clients.
- Industry revenue, shipment counts, the NAM firm count and XPO figures come from search summaries because the pages blocked fetches.
- No ruling on §14101(b) waivers and the 180-day window.
- LanePilot's team size, traction and paid prices are unknown.
- The mentor-network fit and the 25,000–70,000 shipper band are my inferences.

objections: 1. THE FRONT DOOR IS ALREADY FREE, IN THREE LAYERS, AND ASHER'S FREE TOOLS ARE NOT A DIFFERENTIATOR. (a) Detect-only free tools: Warp's free reweigh/reclass checker recalculates density from dimensions, tiers findings into dispute/review/note, and flags fees billed with no weight or class change and duplicate PRO billing (wearewarp.com/tools/reweigh-reclass-audit). LanePilot's free plan gives 7 audits a month plus statute-cited dispute letters (2 a month free). Lojistic's free audit is 'forever'. (b) Audit bundled into the freight-buying platform: FreightSimple says 'free to use,' 'no minimum shipments,' 1000+ manufacturing and distribution customers, 'we audit all bills and challenge incorrect charges on your behalf,' plus guaranteed pricing (freightsimple.com, /pricing). Warp TMS is labeled free for shippers. (c) Contingency with a free first audit: Eller Audit, 'Your first audit is free,' fixed 15%. START-HERE's 'three asks that cost nothing' (class calculator, browser invoice checker) is the same thing Warp gives away. Those are table stakes, not a hook. The 2025 NMFC density-scale edge is a temporary staleness gap that any competitor closes by updating a table.

2. THE SEGMENT THAT HAS NO FREE OR BUNDLED OPTION IS NARROW, AND IT MAY BE UNREACHABLE. Small shippers who buy LTL through a broker or platform (FreightSimple, Warp, WWEX/Unishippers, MyCarrier) get audit as a bundled feature, and 'guaranteed pricing' removes much of the surprise-accessorial problem at the source (the broker eats the variance). Shippers with their own TMS get LanePilot-style checks free. What is left is owner-run firms with direct carrier accounts, no TMS, and about $500k-$5M LTL spend. That is the same pool Eller and Lojistic's contingency tiers chase. Worse for Asher's own prospect list: the dossier cites TForce saying only the payer of the original charges can file. If a prospect's carrier invoices are paid or billed through a broker, Asher cannot file the claim at all. The 42 callable prospects (SJF, Petersen, Kyana, etc.) have not been screened for 'direct carrier account vs broker-billed.' If a large share are broker-billed, the effective list is much shorter than 42. The only broker-share number I found is a 2013 Transport Topics piece (brokers/3PLs near one quarter of LTL revenue), so I cannot size this today.

3. 'WILL THEY PAY 20%' IS NOT THE REAL PROBLEM, BUT THE PRICE ANCHOR IS BELOW HIM AND HE HAS NO PREMIUM TO CHARGE. 20% is inside the observed range: Lojistic charges 29% contingency-only, 19% plus $99/mo, 9% plus $389/mo; AP recovery audits are quoted at 20-30%. But Eller publishes 'Fixed. Always.' 15%, adds 'Most freight auditors charge 30-50%,' and gives the first audit free. So a buyer comparing Asher (20%, no track record, 18 years old, zero references) against Eller (15%, free first audit, 'several hundred LTL contracts reviewed,' named founder) loses on both price and credibility. LanePilot positions on the other pole: software-only, does 'not file on your behalf,' and per a GetApp listing never takes a percentage of recovery. The realistic landing zone is 15% or less with a free first look, which compresses the dossier's own fee table further (about $100-600 a year at $100k spend; about $500-3,000 at $500k).

4. HIS CLAIMED DIFFERENTIATOR, DOCUMENT-GROUNDED ACCESSORIAL VERIFICATION, IS ALREADY ELLER'S PITCH. Eller's LTL page says accessorials are checked against the BOL and delivery receipts ('A liftgate charge is enforceable if the delivery receipt shows the consignee had no dock'), maintains an MRA (pricing agreement) library for every major carrier, drafts disputes citing the MRA clause, NMFC item and 49 USC 13710, files through the carrier's claims portal, and puts human review on any variance over $5. That is Asher's START-HERE objection-handling ('the big firms check the rate file; I check the BOL') almost word for word, from a firm that claims decades of experience. Separately, the accessorial error class is the biggest slice (42.8% of errors per AFS) and is the one most exposed to carrier-side data: Shiplify says 21 of the top 25 LTL carriers use its location database, partnered with FreightSnap (2026-07-01), and claims about one disputed accessorial per 1,000 lookups. All of that is vendor-reported and unaudited, but if even partly true, wrong liftgate/limited-access charges get rarer and carriers get better evidence to win the disputes that remain.

5. THE TECHNOLOGY EDGE (AI + FAST SHIPPING) IS THE THING THE WHOLE MARKET NOW HAS. An agent skill that audits freight invoices against rate cards, accessorial evidence and duplicates sells for $19 on Agensi (it states it does not handle reweighs, class changes or minutes of tariff interpretation, which is exactly where Asher's checks add value, but the gap is rule-writing, not a moat). Warp publishes a paste-in AI prompt that 'drafts the dispute, line by line.' LanePilot drafts statute-cited dispute letters free. Transflo launched Workflow AI for LTL (invoice validation and exception resolution, brokers/carriers; named a digital freight audit solution of the year in June 2026). Lighthouz (YC S24) automates FTL/LTL bill audit and dispute filing for brokers. Opereit raised a $2.5M seed (June 2026) for AI agents that detect overbilling and file claims to resolution 'with no human in the loop' (Europe first). Asher's real edge is 19 checks and 1,143 tests, which took weeks; a funded competitor or a shipper with Claude and a CSV can replicate most of the detection in days. What stays scarce is trust, filing labor and carrier-by-carrier procedure knowledge, and an 18-year-old with 10-15 hours a week has the least of all three.

6. THE 'AI STARTUP MOVES DOWN-MARKET' SCENARIO IS UNDERWAY, AND IT RESOLVES TO FREE, NOT TO 'CHEAPER CONTINGENCY.' Intelligent Audit launched Catalyst (June 2025) for businesses with $15M-$150M revenue, with a 90-day free trial and subscription tiers (parcel only so far; traction disputed by a competitor). Loop raised a $95M Series C (2026-04-17) to build a Logistics Data Platform on its DUX document-extraction models, which is the 'AI reads BOLs and PODs' thesis at scale; I found no SMB product from Loop, but its documents-to-reconciliation stack is exactly what would let it serve a $300k shipper at near-zero marginal cost. When the marginal cost of an audit approaches zero, vendors compete by giving detection away and charging for filing assist or subscription (Lojistic's ladder, LanePilot's quote-credit pricing, Intelligent Audit's 90-day trial). A 20% contingency on a $300 annual fee cannot win against free plus a paid tier. A small LTL recovery shop is then a tuck-in at best (Cass/AcuAudit Jan 2025, Trax/EM6 Nov 2025, AFS/DTA 2022 were platform deals; I found no multiples and nothing for a 30-50 client shop).

7. SMALL-TICKET CLAIMS CARRY FIXED FRICTION THAT EATS A 20% FEE. At typical accessorial charges (the project's own FACT-CHECK says liftgate $75-200), 20% is roughly $15-40 per claim [est]. Against that: XPO requires the invoice paid first, the BOL and delivery receipt, and a submission format (up to 100 PROs); TForce says only the payer can file and quotes a 120-day decision window; and the project's own carrier-claim-channels.md quotes Old Dominion's tariff note that the carrier 'at its option, will apply a charge of $50.00 on settled overcharge claims that were through no fault of Carrier,' which on a shipper-caused reclass or wrong-weight BOL exceeds the whole recovery (I did not re-verify the ODFL tariff text at the carrier's site). Filing is per-carrier, per-issue (49 CFR 378.3(b) grouping), so each small claim is a separate letter and file number. The business only works as a batch operation with consistent client volume, and the dossier's own estimate is that about 20 clients yield about $60k a year before denials.

8. THE ECONOMICS OF THE $500 DIAGNOSTIC ARE UPSIDE-DOWN FOR THE TARGET, AND THE PLAYBOOK IS INCONSISTENT. One month of invoices at $100k annual spend is about $8k; even a 1.5% hit is about $125, so the $500 is rarely earned below about $400k of spend, and START-HERE (updated 2026-10-25) now offers a no-charge first look while 96-hour-plan.md and HANDOFF.md still say $500 flat. Meanwhile three competitors (Eller, Lojistic, LanePilot) all offer a free first look. If the offer is free-first, Asher is selling the same product as Eller at a higher percentage with less proof.

9. COMPETITORS WILL KNOW HIS NUMBERS ARE WEAK. START-HERE's call script still opens with 'industry estimates put billing errors in the five to ten percent range,' which the project's own FACT-CHECK graded WEAK. The best published LTL number I could find is AFS's 4.5% of about 250,000 invoices, and Eller's own page cites median recovery of 2-5% of spend (unsupported win rates). A buyer who has talked to Eller or Lojistic will hear lower, more specific numbers. The retaliation concern (shippers fearing carriers will penalize them) is plausible for a small shipper that depends on carrier capacity; I found evidence only from ocean shipping (FMC) and none for LTL, so it is an unmeasured risk, not a disproved one.

Always.', 'Most freight auditors charge 30-50%', first audit free, BOL/delivery-receipt checks, MRA library, files via carrier claims portal, human review over $5; no minimum stated; example is a $12M LTL program), Lojistic pricing (free plan = ongoing audit, 'All modes supported,' 100 rolling days, 5-year history $49/mo; refund recovery appears only in paid tiers: 29% contingency, $99/mo+19%, $389/mo+9%, $5,959/mo+0%), Lojistic FAQ (lists FTL & LTL auditing; says LTL typically has a six-month statute of limitations), LanePilot home (free plan 5 quotes and 7 audits a month; dispute letters on every plan, 2 a month free; 'is a software tool, not a broker, and does not file on your behalf'; Warehouse $119/mo; 'Built by Aaron... nearly a decade inside LTL freight'), Warp free reweigh/reclass tool and Warp AI-invoice-audit page (free tool, 'drafts the dispute line by line,' examples at about $3M freight spend, Warp TMS 'free for shippers'), FreightSimple home and /pricing (free to use, no minimums, 1000+ manufacturing/distribution customers, guaranteed pricing, automatic bill auditing that challenges incorrect charges), Opereit funding article on Dealroom ($2.5M seed, Seedcamp and Yellow, no-human-in-the-loop claims agents, Europe), Agensi $19 freight invoice rate-card auditor skill, ShipScience 'Loop alternatives' page (a competitor's blog; used only to list who exists), and the project's own dossier, offer-v2, START-HERE, HANDOFF, FACT-CHECK and carrier-claim-channels.md.

KEY URLS: https://www.elleraudit.com/ltl-freight-audit ; https://www.elleraudit.com/savings-calculator ; https://lojistic.com/pricing ; https://www.lojistic.com/shipping-faqs/ftl-ltl-ocean-rail-air-freight-audit-questions ; https://lanepilottech.com/ ; https://www.wearewarp.com/tools/reweigh-reclass-audit ; https://www.wearewarp.com/ai-freight-invoice-audit ; https://www.freightsimple.com/pricing ; https://dealroom.co/news/131056-opereit-raises-2-5m-seed-to-fix-logistics-1b-claims-blind-spot/ ; https://www.agensi.io/skills/freight-invoice-rate-card-auditor ; https://www.transflo.com/news/transflo-unveils-workflow-ai-for-ltl/ ; https://www.loop.com/article/loop-raises-95m-series-c-to-scale-its-ai-platform-across-the-supply-chain ; https://freightsnap.com/freightsnap-and-shiplify-partner-to-build-greater-trust-in-ltl-freight/ ; https://www.intelligentaudit.com/products/catalyst-for-smbs ; https://afs.net/blog/stats-incredible-common-ltl-invoice-errors/ .

WEAKER ITEMS (search summaries only, page blocked or unfetched; treat as leads): MyCarrier 'Freight Audit Pro' launch for SMB shippers (July 2023 BusinessWire; fetch returned 403; MyCarrier is a small/mid-shipper LTL platform with 5,000+ SaaS customers per a 2022 TechCrunch article I did fetch, which listed audit as a roadmap item then); Intelligent Audit Catalyst details (June 2025, $15M-$150M revenue, 90-day free trial, parcel carriers; from search summaries plus a competitor's blog, so traction claims are unverified); WWEX offering a 'complimentary' invoice review at first meeting (search summary; the fetched WWEX audit page did NOT state it was free or that it covers LTL); LanePilot's late-August 2026 launch and 'never a percentage of recovery' pricing (GetApp listing summary; vendor page does not state either); the 2013 broker/3PL share of LTL revenue; Shiplify's 21-of-25 carriers and dispute-rate claims (vendor-reported). The ODFL $50 charge is quoted from the project's own carrier-claim-channels.md, not re-fetched at ODFL.

CORRECTIONS TO THE DOSSIER: Lojistic's free tier says 'All modes supported' but does not name LTL, and refund recovery is not in the free plan, so 'free forever LTL audit' is slightly overstated; the free plan is detection, and recovery is paid. Eller's 15% is on the savings-calculator page, not the LTL page, and I could not confirm Eller serves owner-run firms under $5M (examples are mid-market).

WHAT I LOOKED FOR AND DID NOT FIND (this cuts in Asher's favor): no US AI freight-audit startup pricing a contingency tier below 20% for sub-$5M LTL shippers; no evidence Loop has an SMB tier; no evidence Freightview, Shipwell or FreightPOP bundle LTL audit (Freightview reportedly has no dedicated audit module); no LTL-specific evidence of carrier retaliation; Lojistic's free tier keeps only 100 days, shorter than the 180-day window, and Warp/LanePilot stop at detection and do not file; Lighthouz, Transflo and Opereit target brokers, carriers or Europe, not US direct shippers. The price range supports 20% as normal. So the whitespace is real but narrow: a done-for-you filing service for owner-run, direct-account, no-TMS shippers at $500k-$5M.

VERDICT: SERIOUS, not fatal. This is a viable side-income service, not a defensible company. The competition is not one rival; it is a price floor of free detection plus bundled audit in the broker/platform channel, plus a 15% specialist with a free first audit, plus a falling cost of AI detection. If the experiment goes ahead, the two cheapest tests that would change my view are (1) screen each of the 42 prospects for broker-billed vs direct carrier accounts before dialing, and (2) ask the first five conversations which free tools (Warp, LanePilot, Lojistic, FreightSimple, WWEX) they already use and whether anyone has already quoted them 15%."

objections: EXECUTION RECORD IS THE BINDING PROBLEM. The system was declared finished around Aug 10. On Oct 25, `track.py pipeline` still reports 42 prospects due and 0 called. `personalize.py --check` still shows 154 unfilled placeholders across 17 files. There is no dist/ build and no clients/ folder. The outreach tracker was last touched Aug 10. The 96-hour plan aimed at $1,000 signed by Aug 13 and was missed. START-HERE.md still opens 'Monday morning' and calls the setup a 25-minute job (PayPal Business account, one command, one drag-and-drop deploy). The mismatch is stark: a 6,062-line engine, 1,143 tests and a 67k-word site against zero conversations. The setup step puts his real full name, phone and face-value age in front of skeptical adults, and that is the step not taken. The cause may be college applications, or reluctance to attach his name. Either way, a founder who has not done the 25-minute step in 10 weeks is unlikely to make roughly 120 cold contacts in the next 6. A business whose only scarce input is the founder's willingness to dial fails on that input.

THE TIME BUDGET DOES NOT MATCH THE JOB. START-HERE says to call 8-10am and 2-4pm prospect-local. A high-school senior with a normal school day (his own calendar shows 7:45am and 3:00pm teacher meetings) can use only the 3-4pm ET slot for Central-time prospects. Everything else lands in class or after the buyer has gone home. Offer-v2 section 1.1 gives Gong's average connect rate of 5.4% and set rate of 4.6%, about 2 meetings per 800 dials. The call script assumes about 8x that connect rate (43%) and about 7x the yes rate. At 42 prospects x 4 attempts, that is roughly 8-9 live conversations and 1-3 invoice senders at best. The dossier's six-week test needs about 120 contacts to land 3 invoice sets. Calls, teardowns, 30/60-day claim chasing and a monthly audit cycle for several carriers is more than 10-15 hours a week in the same autumn as ED/Nov 1 applications and Q1 grades. The weeks that matter most for the test overlap finals (May-June 2027) and then the move to college (Aug 2027).

THE OFFER LEAKS AND THE FEE IS HARD TO COLLECT. The free teardown and the $500 report already contain 'the claim drafted and ready to file' (engagement-terms.md). Part 378 lets the shipper file for itself, and carriers only care who paid the original charge. A client can take the findings and file without Asher. Under the 20% contingency, a refund arrives as a credit memo on the client's own carrier account, where Asher has no visibility. Collection relies on the client reporting it ('notification when a carrier pays'), invoiced monthly Net 15. At the dossier's per-client math the fee is about $100-$600 a year at $100k LTL spend and $500-$3,000 at $500k. That is below the cost of chasing a non-payer, and it is paid by a customer who owes nothing to an 18-year-old with no references. ODFL also adds a $50 charge on settled overcharge claims (carrier-claim-channels.md line 66), which eats small recoveries. Free alternatives sit in the same niche (Warp, Lojistic free tier, LanePilot, Eller's first audit free).

THE DOSSIER'S LEGAL SECTION HAS A HOLE: STATE COLLECTION-AGENCY LICENSING. It checked only the FMCSA broker definition (49 CFR 371.2). It did not check whether a person who collects money owed to others, for a cut, needs a state collection licence. The closest primary evidence is a Minnesota Office of Administrative Hearings recommendation (Oct 9, 2024, PurCo Fleet Services). It applied Minn. Stat. 332.33, 'engaged in the business of collection for others any account, bill, or other indebtedness'. It covered a firm that recovers money its clients are owed and keeps a share, held that licensing was required, and noted a Nov 2023 cease-and-desist. The firm had rewritten its contracts from 'collect' to 'recover' and still lost. A freight auditor who recovers carrier overcharges for a percentage fits that wording on its face. I found no freight-audit exemption. Weaker, unverified leads: a Tennessee board position that B2B collection needs a licence (search summary; the TN page returned 403), and a trade-source claim that about 20 states license commercial collectors. I found no enforcement against a freight auditor, and many statutes are consumer-focused. So this is unpriced and unresolved, not proven fatal. The usual consequences (cease-and-desist, penalties, and in some states a bar on enforcing the fee contract) land hardest on the contingency fee, which is the only scalable revenue.

NO ESCALATION POWER, SO CARRIERS CAN SIMPLY SAY NO. Filing a Part 378 claim as an authorized agent is fine (49 CFR 378.2 defines 'claimant' to include the shipper's authorized agent). Unauthorized-practice-of-law risk is low for that step because a carrier is not a tribunal. Wisconsin ethics opinion E-79-3 treats freight-bill auditing as technical work and advocacy before tribunals as law. The risk rises on any escalation. RUNBOOK stage 7b ends with the civil-action dates 'goes to a transportation attorney now'. No attorney will take a $400-$3,000 claim on contingency, and carriers know a one-person auditor cannot sue. Reclass and reweigh disputes are decided by the carrier's own scale and inspection record. An unnamed LTL executive told FreightWaves in Dec 2018: 'We don't find many reweighs in favor of the customer.' The 180-day rule itself is not settled national law. The 10th Circuit decided Southern Furniture Leasing v. YRC over a dissent, and the project's own site admits it is 'one circuit'. A 14101(b) pricing-agreement waiver could make a client's deadline contractual, and I found no case either way. The realistic win rate on contested claims is therefore unmeasured and may be well below the vendor figures (70-82%).

MISSED DEADLINES ARE PERMANENT LOSSES, WITH NO BACKSTOP. The clock is a rolling 180 days per invoice, and carriers set it differently: Central Transport runs it from the carrier's receipt of the shipment, YRC from pickup, and TForce counts receipt as 10 days after tender. ODFL closes a claim in 30 days and allows a single shot. XPO requires the invoice to be paid first, and Transwood allows only the original payer to file. A monthly service therefore creates a standing duty for each client. If Asher is in finals, on a trip or at orientation, that month's errors expire and the client's money is gone. He is the only staff, with no entity named in the contract, no E&O insurance and no attorney review. The contract itself says to spend 'a few hundred dollars' on an attorney review before five-figure contingency deals. That has not been done. In August 2027 he leaves for college and the service has no continuity plan.

UNVERIFIED ACCURACY ON REAL CARRIER DATA. HANDOFF.md's own rule is 'a false finding costs more than a missed one'. FACT-CHECK found 13 of 18 rows of the density-class table wrong, the '18 months' lookback wrong, a fabricated '30% claims abandoned' quote, and error statistics with no source. All of that was found by auditing his own materials, not by a client. The 1,143 tests and the 'zero findings on clean freight' calibration come from synthetic or constructed populations built by the same author and AI agents. No real client invoice or carrier response has ever run through the engine. The first false accessorial claim against a real PRO costs credibility with a carrier claims desk and with a small circle of shippers who talk. There is some legal tail too: in the First Circuit's Blanchette v. Cataldo (1984), a non-lawyer freight-claims agent who filed about 1,900 claims he later withdrew took a $76,000 Chapter 93A judgment, which was affirmed. That is a railroad-era analogy only.

THE TRUST ASK IS THE HARDEST PART FOR A TEENAGER. The target buyer is an owner or controller at a $5-100M manufacturer. The first ask is to email invoices and, ideally, the carrier rate agreement to an anonymous 18-year-old with no entity, clients, references or insurance certificate. Rate agreements are usually confidential (Lojistic says all UPS and FedEx contracts carry confidentiality clauses; I found no LTL-specific text). The project's own site tells the buyer to verify him from a reference library, which helps but is not a reference. The contract promises 'I don't share them', so any use of a third-party LLM API on client PDFs needs disclosure to be literally true. The dossier's suggestion to add a de-identified data-asset clause makes the trust ask harder, not easier. Mentor introductions are the only credible route and none has been used.

(2) Minnesota OAH PurCo Fleet Services recommendation, 2024-10-09, read via pdftotext (https://mn.gov/oah/assets/1002-39748-purco-fleet-services-commerce-unlicensed-debt-collection-summary-disposition-order_tcm19-649392.pdf). It is an ALJ recommendation; I did not see the Commissioner's final order. (3) Wisconsin E-79-3, read via pdftotext (https://wisbar.org/formembers/ethics/Ethics%20Opinions/E-79-3.pdf). It is from 1979 and may be superseded. (4) FreightWaves 2018-12-17 executive quote confirmed on fetch (https://www.freightwaves.com/news/ltl-suit-against-yrc-spotlights-reweighing-practices). (5) Transwood claims page: only the original payer may file (https://www.transwood.com/customers/loss-damage-claims/). (6) Blanchette v. Cataldo, fetched summary (https://hallapproved.com/us/cases/ca1/1984/435920/): Penn Central's unauthorized-practice claim was not resolved; the Chapter 93A judgment of $76,000 was affirmed.

WEAK OR UNVERIFIED (search-summary only): the Tennessee Collection Service Board position on B2B licensing (support.commerce.tn.gov FAQ returned 403); 'about 20 states license commercial collectors' (trade-association source via search summary); Central/YRC/Pitt Ohio deadline wording (consistent with the project's carrier-claim-channels.md); Lojistic's UPS/FedEx confidentiality statement. No search found any court decision applying or refusing a 14101(b) waiver to the 180-day window, matching the dossier. I found no source on freight-audit collection licensing either way, which is the gap itself.

WHAT DID NOT HOLD UP (calibration, so the critique stays honest): federal law permits an agent to file Part 378 claims, and I found no federal licence or bond requirement for pure invoice auditing. The FMCSA broker definition is only triggered if he arranges transportation, and the contract bars rate negotiation. He is a legal adult, with 19 in Alabama and Nebraska and 21 in Mississippi per the dossier's secondary source. The collection-licensing and unauthorized-practice-of-law risks are unresolved rather than shown fatal. No enforcement against a freight auditor turned up.

WHY 'SERIOUS' AND NOT 'FATAL': the cost to test is close to zero. It takes one 25-minute setup and six weeks of free teardowns, which do not trigger a contingency contract. The kill risk sits in founder behavior and fee economics, not in a confirmed legal bar.

WHAT WOULD CHANGE MY MIND, and a stop rule: (a) the setup done and 40 logged dials within 14 days. If not, shelve it, because nothing downstream is reachable. (b) A one-hour consult with a transportation or collection attorney in his state on collection licensing, plus an LLC and an E&O quote, before the first contingency contract. (c) Three real invoice sets showing at least 1% of spend collectible, per the dossier's own test."
